Learning Objectives
1. Describe the embryologic development of the central nervous system, including
neurulation, neural tube formation, and differentiation of the brain and spinal cord,
and relate these processes to mature neuroanatomy. (CLO 1)
2. Describe the embryologic development of the pharyngeal apparatus and relate its
derivatives to clinically relevant head and neck structures. (CLO 1)
3. Correlate abnormalities in neural and craniofacial development with common
congenital disorders involving the central nervous system and head and neck.
(CLO 3)
Pre-Session Assignment
• Preview the PowerPoint slides. You are not expected to memorize details before class.

Development of the Neural Tube
• Begins in week 3 → neural plate & groove
• Notochord induces ectoderm → neural plate
• Signals: TGF-β, Wnts, SHH, BMPs
• Neural folds fuse → neural tube (CNS)
• Neural crest → PNS & ANS structures
Sequence (see image)
• Neural plate
• Neural groove + folds
• Fusion → neural tube + neural crest
Neural plate and folding leading to neural tube formation. (A) Neural plate (day
17). (B) Early neural groove and folds. (C) Fusion begins (day 22), still open at
both ends. (D–F) Transverse sections show closure, tube separation from
ectoderm, and neural crest formation. Fig 16.1 BWAB, 11e.

Neurulation (Week 4)
Neural tube first closes in the future cervical region. Fig. 16.2 (A) Day 23: neural folds fuse to form the neural tube. (B) Day 24:
The neural folds close in zipper-like fashion in both directions. forebrain prominence and rostral neuropore closing. BWAB, 11e.
• Neural folds fuse → neural tube • Rostral neuropore closes ~day 25
• Neural canal is open at both ends • Caudal neuropore closes ~day 27
Neural tube → Brain and Spinal Cord
Neural Canal → Ventricular System

Failure of Neural Tube Closure
Anencephaly Neural Tube Defect
Failure of closure of anterior neuropore Failure of closure of posterior neuropore
Images: Carlson Fig 8-4, Larsen Fig 4-11

Spina Bifida
Spina Bifida Occulta
• Failure of fusion of posterior vertebral arches
• Spinal cord and meninges remain intact
• Usually asymptomatic; may have overlying tuft of hair
• Typically lumbosacral; often discovered incidentally
Meningocele
• Herniation of meninges and CSF through vertebral defect
• No spinal cord tissue in the sac
• Neurological deficits usually absent
Myelomeningocele
• Herniation of meninges and spinal cord through vertebral defect
• Most commonly lumbosacral
• Lower limb motor/sensory deficits and bowel/bladder dysfunction
• Risk of infection if neural tissue is exposed
Occulta: Bony defect only | Meningocele: Meninges + CSF | Myelomeningocele: Meninges + spinal cord
American Association of Neurological Surgeons

Cervical Meningocele Myelomeningocele
Internet Scientific Publication
Moore. Before We Are Born

Neural Tube Defects (NTDs): Risk Factors & Prevention
Neural Tube Closure: Normally completed by day 28 of embryonic development
Folate deficiency: Major risk factor during early pregnancy
Folic acid supplementation: Before conception and during early pregnancy reduces NTD risk
Antiseizure medications: Valproic acid and carbamazepine increase NTD risk
Genetic susceptibility: increased concordance in monozygotic twins

Anencephaly & Holoprosencephaly
Anencephaly
• Failure of anterior (rostral) neuropore closure during week 4
• Absence of most of the cerebral hemispheres and calvarium
• Severe, typically lethal neural tube defect
• Associated with folate deficiency
Holoprosencephaly
• Failure of the prosencephalon to divide into cerebral hemispheres
• Severe forms associated with midline facial defects (e.g., cyclopia)
• Associated with SHH signaling abnormalities and trisomy 13
Anencephaly = failure of neural tube closure | Holoprosencephaly = failure of forebrain division
Pregmed.org

Other Disorders of Brain Development
Lissencephaly
• Abnormal neuronal migration → reduced or absent cerebral gyri (smooth brain)
• Associated with developmental delay, seizures, and intellectual disability
• Classic genetic associations: LIS1 (PAFAH1B1) and DCX
Microcephaly
• Abnormally small head circumference due to impaired brain growth
Robbins and Cotran Pathology
• Associated with genetic abnormalities and congenital infections (e.g., Zika virus)
• May cause developmental delay and intellectual disability
Lissencephaly = abnormal neuronal migration
Microcephaly = impaired brain growth
Adam
Pharyngeal Apparatus

Neural Crest → Pharyngeal Arches
Fig. 17.2 Migrations pathways on neural crest cells
into the pharyngeal arches and face.
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.
• Neural crest cells migrate from neural tube
• Populate pharyngeal arches, which form head & neck structures
• Give rise to skeletal, vascular, and connective tissue elements

Pharyngeal Apparatus Overview
• Components = arches + pouches + clefts
• Timing: forms during weeks 4–7
• Function: gives rise to most head & neck structures
• Clinical note: errors → congenital anomalies
Fig. 17.3 Development of the Pharyngeal arches. A. 25 days. B. 28 Days. C. 5 weeks
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Arch 1 (Mandibular Arch)
• Skeletal Derivatives: mandible, malleus, incus
• Muscles: mastication, mylohyoid, anterior
digastric, tensors (tensor tympani, tensor veli
palatini)
• Nerve: CN V (mandibular nerve)
3
• Clinical: Treacher Collins (first arch defect;
mandibular hypoplasia, hearing loss)
Fig. 17.9 Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of
the various pharyngeal arches. Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Arch 2 (Hyoid Arch)
• Skeletal Derivatives: stapes, styloid, lesser hyoid horn
• Muscles: Facial expression, stapedius, posterior
digastric, stylohyoid
• Nerve: CN VII
• Pathology: Conductive hearing loss (stapes fixation)
Fig. 17.9 Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of
the various pharyngeal arches. Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Arch 3 (Glossopharyngeal Arch)
• Skeletal Derivative: Greater hyoid horn
• Muscle: Stylopharyngeus
• Nerve: CN IX
• Pathology: Loss of gag reflex (afferent)
Fig. 17.9 Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of
the various pharyngeal arches. Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Arches 4 & 6 (Laryngeal Arches)
• Skeletal Derivatives: Laryngeal framework
• Muscles: muscles of larynx, most muscles of
pharynx and soft palate
• Nerve: CN X
• Pathology: dysphagia, pharyngeal weakness,
hoarseness
Fig. 17.9 Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of
the various pharyngeal arches. Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Blue structures

Fig. 17.1 Skeletal structures of the head and face.
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Agnathia
• Cause: failure of neural crest cells to populate 1st arch
• Severe 1st arch malformation (extreme hypoplasia)
• Mandible fails to form (absent lower jaw)
• Rare, often incompatible with life

Treacher Collins Syndrome – Clinical Features
(Mandibulofacial Dysostosis; 1st Arch Syndrome)
• Cause: Abnormal development and survival of neural crest cells contributing to the first pharyngeal arch
• Genetics: Most commonly TCOF1 mutation; usually autosomal dominant
Craniofacial Abnormalities
• Mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia
• Downward-slanting palpebral fissures
• External ear and ossicular malformations
• Clinical: Conductive hearing loss; variable severity
Failure of first arch neural crest migration
→ craniofacial malformations + conductive hearing loss

Pierre Robin Sequence
Sequence
• Initial abnormality: Mandibular hypoplasia (micrognathia)
• Glossoptosis: Posterior displacement of the tongue
• Cleft palate: Tongue interferes with normal palatal shelf elevation and fusion
• Clinical: Upper airway obstruction and feeding difficulties
Micrognathia → Glossoptosis → Cleft Palate

Pharyngeal Apparatus: Arches, Pouches & Clefts
Pharyngeal Arches
• External ectoderm, internal endoderm, and mesenchymal core
• Each arch contains cartilage, muscle, nerve, and artery components
Pharyngeal Pouches
• Endoderm-lined internal out-pocketings
• Form structures including the thymus, parathyroids,
and middle ear cavity
Pharyngeal Clefts
• Ectoderm-lined external grooves
• First cleft → external acoustic meatus
• Remaining clefts normally disappear
Fig. 17.6 Pharyngeal arches sectioned
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.
(Modified with Photoshop to show correct first arch germ layer.)

Pouches
• 1st Pouch: Middle ear, Eustachian tube
• 2nd Pouch: Palatine tonsils
• 3rd Pouch: Thymus, inferior parathyroids
• 4th Pouch: Superior parathyroids, C cells
(via ultimobranchial body)
Clinical
• DiGeorge (3rd/4th pouch) → T-cell deficiency, hypocalcemia
Fig. 17.11 Migration of the thymus, parathyroid glands and the
ultimobranchial body. Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Branchial (Pharyngeal) Clefts
• 1st cleft → external auditory canal
• 2nd–4th clefts → normally obliterate
• Clinical: persistence → branchial cleft cysts / fistula
Fig. 17.6 Pharyngeal arches sectioned
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.
(Modified to show correct first arch germ layer.) Fig. 17.11 Migration of the thymus, parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Branchial Cleft Cyst (Lateral Cervical Cyst)
• Persistent 2nd cleft
• Branchial cleft cyst, sinus, or fistula
• Lateral neck mass, anterior to SCM
Cervical sinus
Cyst = closed cavity
Sinus = one opening (external or internal)
Fistula – two openings (skin pharynx)
Fig. 17.10 Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Thyroid Development
• Origin: Endodermal evagination (week 4)
at foramen cecum (tongue base)
• Migration: Descends via thyroglossal duct
• Final Position: Duct degenerates →
thyroid isolated in neck
• Not derived from pharyngeal arches
Fig. 17.11 Migration of the thymus, parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Clinical: Thyroid Development
Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
• Failure of thyroglossal duct regression
• Midline mass, moves with
swallowing/tongue protrusion
Ectopic/Lingual Thyroid
• Thyroid tissue at tongue base
Fig. 17.11 Migration of the thymus, parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body
Langman’s Medical Embryology,13e.

Thyroglossal Duct Cyst vs. Branchial Cleft Cyst
• Thyroglossal duct cyst: Midline, moves with swallowing
• Branchial Cyst: Lateral neck, does not move with swallowing
Development of the Face

Facial Prominences

1st arch
Frontal views of embryo at the end of the 24 Day (A) and 30 days (B)
Failure of Fusion
• Face forms from 5 prominences
→ cleft lip, cleft palate, facial clefts
• Frontonasal → forehead, nose, philtrum
• Maxillary (2) → cheeks, lateral portions of upper lip
• Mandibular (2) → lower lip, mandible
• Medial nasal prominences → merge to form the intermaxillary segment, including the philtrum

Development of the Face
Intermaxillary
segment
Face Development: 5th and 6th week Face Development: 7th and 10th week
• Nasal placodes develop into medial and lateral nasal prominences
• Medial nasal prominences merge → intermaxillary segment (philtrum)
• Maxillary + medial nasal prominences → formation of upper lip
• Lateral nasal prominences → sides (alae) of nose
• Failure of maxillary–medial nasal fusion → cleft lip
Medial nasal + maxillary prominences → upper lip | Failure of fusion → cleft lip
Fig. 17.22, 17.23. LME

Palate Formation
Primary Palate
• Develops from the intermaxillary segment (merged medial
nasal prominences)
• Forms the small anterior portion of the hard palate, anterior
Primary and Secondary Palate
to the incisive foramen
Secondary Palate
• Develops from palatal shelves of the maxillary prominences
• Shelves elevate and fuse at the midline
• Forms the remaining hard palate and soft palate
Final Fusion
• Secondary palate joins the primary palate and nasal septum
Fusion of Nasal Septum with Palate
Primary palate = medial nasal prominences | Secondary palate = maxillary prominences

Palate Formation: Stepwise Sequence
Step 1 — Initial Position
• Palatal shelves grow vertically alongside the tongue
Step 2 — Elevation
• Tongue descends; palatal shelves elevate into a
horizontal position
Step 3 — Fusion
• Shelves fuse at the midline and with the primary palate
and nasal septum
• Separates the developing oral and nasal cavities

between maxillary and medial
nasal prominences

shelf fusion or fusion with the

Visual System
Structure, Visual Pathways, and Reflexes
Aftab Merchant, MBBS, FCPS, MHPE
Professor of Medical Education
Assistant Dean of Anatomical Education
Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine
University of Nevada Las Vegas

Learning Objectives (2026)
1. Describe the structure and optical properties of the eye and relate them to image formation.
(CLO 1, CLO 2)
2. Explain the organization of the retina and visual pathway from photoreceptors to the visual
cortex, and correlate lesions along the pathway with characteristic visual field deficits. (CLO
1, CLO 2, CLO 3)
3. Correlate the neural pathways underlying visual reflexes with normal ocular function and
common neurological disorders. (CLO 2, CLO 3)
Pre-Session Assignment
• Preview the PowerPoint slides. You are not expected to memorize details before class.
• Boards & Beyond B&B: Eye Anatomy (26 min)
• B&B: Retina (14 min)
• B&B: Visual Field Defects (13 min)
Eye Structure & Image Formation

Layers of the Eyeball
Fibrous (Outer) Layer
• Sclera: protection and extraocular muscle attachment
• Cornea: transparent, major refractive surface
Vascular (Middle) Layer — Uvea
• Choroid: vascular supply to outer retina
• Ciliary body: aqueous humor production and
accommodation
• Iris: regulates pupil size
Neural (Inner) Layer
• Retina: detects light and initiates visual signaling
Fig. 8.105 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.
Fibrous = protection/refraction | Vascular = nutrition/control | Neural = vision

Cornea, Lens, Image Formation
• Cornea: provides approximately two-thirds of the eye's refractive power
• Lens: adjusts refractive power for near and distant vision
• Light rays converge on the retina, forming an inverted and reversed image
• Fovea centralis: region of highest visual acuity
Cornea = major refraction | Lens = adjustable focus | Retina = image detection
conceptviz.app

Ciliary Body & Accommodation
Distant Vision
• Ciliary muscle relaxes → zonular fibers tighten
• Lens flattens → lower refractive power
Near Vision
• Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibers loosen
• Lens becomes rounder → higher refractive power
Innervation
• Parasympathetic: CN III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves
Near vision: ciliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds

Iris & Pupillary Control
Iris: pigmented diaphragm controlling pupil size
Sphincter Pupillae
• Parasympathetic: CN III → ciliary ganglion
→ short ciliary nerves
• Contraction → miosis (pupil constriction)
Dilator Pupillae
• Sympathetic: superior cervical ganglion
→ long ciliary nerves (principal route)
• Contraction → mydriasis (pupil dilation)
Fig. 8.103 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e. .
Champney. ECNA, 2016.

Retina, Macula, Fovea & Optic Disc
Retina
• Neural layer responsible for light detection
• Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve (CN II)
Macula Lutea
• Central retinal region responsible for detailed vision
• Fovea centralis: highest cone density and visual acuity
Optic Disc
• Exit of optic nerve and central retinal vessels
• No photoreceptors → physiological blind spot
Fovea = highest visual acuity | Optic disc = blind spot
Fundus

Papilledema
Normal Papilledema

Visual Fields & Visual Pathways
Each cerebral hemisphere processes information from the opposite visual hemifield.

Visual Fields vs Retinal Fields
Visual Field
• Area of space visible while looking straight ahead
• Divided into right/left and superior/inferior visual fields
Retinal Field
• Image projected onto the retina is inverted and reversed
• Left visual field → right half of each retina
• Right visual field → left half of each retina
• Superior visual field → inferior retina
Visual field and retinal location are opposite
Siegel, Essential Neuroscience

Nasal vs Temporal Hemiretina
• Each retina is divided into nasal and temporal hemiretinae
• Temporal visual field → nasal retina
• Nasal visual field → temporal retina
• Each eye receives information from both visual hemifields
• Binocular visual fields overlap centrally
Temporal visual field → nasal retina
Nasal visual field → temporal retina
Siegel, Essential Neuroscience

Visual Pathway: Retina to Cortex
• Retinal ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve (CN II)
• Optic nerves converge at the optic chiasm
• Fibers continue as optic tracts
• Most fibers synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus
• Optic radiations project to the primary visual cortex (V1)
Retina → CN II → Chiasm → Optic tract → LGN → Optic radiations → V1
The Visual Pathway
Berger. CCNA

Optic Chiasm: Which Fibers Cross?
• Nasal retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm
• Temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral
• Each optic tract carries information from the contralateral visual hemifield
• Right optic tract → left visual field
• Left optic tract → right visual field
Nasal fibers CROSS | Temporal fibers STAY
Which visual hemifield is carried by the right optic tract?
The Visual Pathway
Berger. CCNA

Lateral Geniculate Nucleus & Optic Radiations
Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
• Visual relay nucleus of the thalamus
• Receives input from the contralateral visual hemifield
• Projects to the primary visual cortex via optic radiations
Optic Radiations
• Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop): inferior retinal fibers → superior visual field
• Parietal lobe: superior retinal fibers → inferior visual field
Meyer's loop → superior visual field
Parietal radiations → inferior visual field
Siegel, Essential Neuroscience

Primary Visual Cortex (V1)
• Located along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe
• Cuneus (superior bank): inferior visual field
• Lingual gyrus (inferior bank): superior visual field
• Occipital pole: central (macular) vision
• More anterior visual cortex represents
peripheral vision
Cuneus = inferior visual field
Lingual gyrus = superior visual field
Siegel, Essential Neuroscience

Visual Pathway: Three Rules for Localization
Rule 1 — Retinal Projection
• Visual fields project to the opposite retinal halves
Rule 2 — Optic Chiasm
• Nasal retinal fibers cross; temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral
Rule 3 — Cerebral Representation
• Each hemisphere processes the contralateral visual hemifield
• Temporal radiations carry superior-field information
• Parietal radiations carry inferior-field information
Visual field → Retina → CN II → Chiasm →
Optic tract → LGN → Optic radiations → Cortex
The Visual Pathway
Berger. CCNA
Visual Field Defects & Lesion Localization

Visual Field Defects: Localization Principles
• Lesions along the visual pathway produce characteristic visual-field deficits
• Prechiasmal lesions: monocular visual loss
• Chiasmal lesions: heteronymous visual-field defects
• Postchiasmal lesions: contralateral homonymous visual-field defects
• Lesion location determines the pattern of visual loss
Before chiasm → monocular
Chiasm → heteronymous
After chiasm → homonymous
Visual Field Defects
Berger. CCNA

Optic Nerve & Optic Chiasm Lesions
Optic Nerve Lesion
• Ipsilateral monocular visual loss
• Loss of visual input from the affected eye
Optic Chiasm Lesion
• Damage to crossing nasal retinal fibers
• Bitemporal hemianopia
• Classically associated with pituitary mass compression
Optic nerve → monocular loss | Optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia
Visual Field Defects
Berger. CCNA

Optic Tract Lesion
• Each optic tract carries information from the contralateral visual hemifield
• Lesion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia
• Both eyes lose the same half of their visual fields
Example
• Right optic tract lesion → left homonymous hemianopia
Right optic tract lesion → left homonymous hemianopia
Visual Field Defects
Berger. CCNA

Optic Radiations: Temporal vs Parietal Lesions
Temporal Lobe — Meyer's Loop
• Carries information from the contralateral superior visual field
• Lesion → contralateral superior quadrantanopia
• Pie in the sky
Parietal Lobe — Superior Optic Radiations
• Carries information from the contralateral inferior visual field
• Lesion → contralateral inferior quadrantanopia
• Pie on the floor
Temporal → superior field loss | Parietal → inferior field loss
Visual Field Defects
Siegel, Berger

Primary Visual Cortex Lesions
• Primary visual cortex (V1) lies along the calcarine sulcus
• Unilateral lesion → contralateral homonymous hemianopia
• Occipital pole: represents central (macular) vision
• Some occipital lesions produce macular sparing
• Common vascular association: posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
Siegel, Essential Neuroscience

Visual and Ocular Reflexes

Pupillary Light Reflex: Neural Pathway
• Function: Regulates light entering the eye through pupillary
constriction (miosis)
• Stimulus: Light entering the retina
• Afferent limb (CN II): Retina → optic nerve → pretectal nuclei
(midbrain)
• Central connection: Pretectal nuclei → bilateral Edinger–
Westphal nuclei
• Efferent limb (CN III): Edinger–Westphal nucleus → CN III →
ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae
• Response: Direct and consensual pupillary constriction
Singh. TCNA, 4e.

Pupillary Light Reflex: CN II vs CN III Lesions
Light in Light in
Lesion
Affected Eye Unaffected Eye
CN II
Neither pupil constricts Both pupils constrict
(afferent)
CN III
Only unaffected pupil constricts Only unaffected pupil constricts
(efferent)
CN II lesion → defective sensory input
CN III lesion → defective pupillary constriction
Singh. TCNA, 4e.

Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (Marcus Gunn Pupil)
• Cause: Reduced sensory input from one eye, commonly due to optic nerve disease
• Test: Swinging flashlight test
• Light in healthy eye → both pupils constrict
• Light moved to affected eye → both pupils dilate relatively (reduced constriction)
• Efferent CN III pathways remain intact
RAPD → Afferent defect (CN II), not an efferent CN III lesion

Near Response (Accommodation–Convergence)
The near response consists of three coordinated changes when shifting focus from a distant to
a near object.
1. Accommodation: Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibers relax → lens becomes rounder
2. Convergence: Medial rectus muscles contract (CN III) → eyes turn inward
3. Pupillary Constriction (Miosis): Sphincter pupillae contracts → reduces pupil diameter
Near response = Accommodation + Convergence + Miosis

Neural Pathways of the Near Response
Afferent Pathway
• Retina → CN II → visual cortex → supranuclear near-response pathways
Efferent Pathways
Parasympathetic (GVE)
• Edinger–Westphal nucleus → CN III → ciliary ganglion
• Ciliary muscle → accommodation
• Sphincter pupillae → miosis
Somatic Motor (GSE)
• Oculomotor nucleus → CN III → medial rectus muscles
• Bilateral eye convergence
CN III coordinates all three components of the near response

Light-Near Dissociation
• Pupillary response to light is impaired
• Pupillary constriction during near fixation is preserved or relatively better
Clinical Associations
• Argyll Robertson pupil: small, irregular pupils; classically associated with neurosyphilis
• Adie's tonic pupil: dilated pupil with slow, sustained near constriction
• Parinaud syndrome: dorsal midbrain lesion disrupting pupillary light-reflex pathways
Light response impaired | Near constriction relatively preserved

Corneal (Blink) Reflex
• Function: Protective reflex producing bilateral eyelid closure
• Stimulus: Light touch of the cornea
• Afferent limb (GSA): CN V1 (nasociliary nerve) → spinal trigeminal nucleus
• Central connections: Trigeminal sensory pathways → bilateral facial motor nuclei
• Efferent limb (SVE): CN VII → orbicularis oculi
• Response: Bilateral blinking (direct + consensual)
Corneal reflex: V1 in → VII out → bilateral blinking

Corneal Reflex: Lesion Localization
Lesion Touch affected cornea Touch unaffected cornea
CN V1 (afferent) Neither eye blinks Both eyes blink
CN VII (efferent) Only unaffected eye blinks Only unaffected eye blinks
Clinical Correlation
• CN V1 lesion: loss of sensory input from affected cornea
• CN VII lesion: impaired ipsilateral eyelid closure (e.g., Bell palsy)

Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR)
• Function: Stabilizes gaze during head movement
• Stimulus: Head rotation detected by semicircular canals
• Afferent limb: Vestibular division of CN VIII
• Central pathway: Vestibular nuclei → CN VI nucleus → MLF → CN III nucleus
• Efferent limb: CN VI (lateral rectus) + CN III (medial rectus)
• Response: Eyes move opposite to head rotation
• Head turns one way → eyes move the opposite way
• VOR stabilizes the retinal image during head movement
without requiring conscious visual processing.
Vestibular Health Website

Oculocephalic Reflex (Doll's Eye Maneuver)
• Assesses vestibular–brainstem–ocular motor pathways in unconscious patients
• Intact VOR: Eyes move opposite to head rotation, maintaining gaze direction in space
• Absent VOR: Eyes remain stationary within the orbits and move with the head
• Abnormal response may indicate brainstem dysfunction
Clinical Precaution
• Do not perform if cervical spine instability is suspected
Eyes move left Eyes stay centered
Schematic: in both examples the head turns right;
the eye positions within the orbits differ.
Oculocephalic reflex = clinical assessment of VOR integrity

Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF)
• Location: Paired white matter tract near the midline of the brainstem
• Connects vestibular nuclei and ocular motor nuclei (CN III, IV, VI)
• Coordinates conjugate eye movements
• Essential for the vestibulo-ocular reflex
• Lesion disrupts coordinated horizontal gaze

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)
• Cause: Lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
• Ipsilateral eye: Impaired adduction during horizontal gaze
• Contralateral eye: Abducting nystagmus
• Convergence: Usually preserved
• Clinical associations: Multiple sclerosis (younger patients), brainstem stroke (older patients)
• Example: Left MLF lesion → left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze
MLF lesion → ipsilateral adduction deficit + contralateral abducting nystagmus

Summary
• Cornea and lens: Refract light and focus images on the retina
• Retina: Detects light; fovea provides highest visual acuity
• Visual pathway: Retina → CN II → chiasm → optic tract → LGN → radiations → V1
• Optic chiasm: Nasal fibers cross; each hemisphere processes the opposite visual field
• Visual field defects: Optic nerve → monocular; chiasm → bitemporal; postchiasmal → homonymous loss
• Pupillary light reflex: CN II → pretectal nuclei → Edinger–Westphal nuclei → CN III
• Near reflex: Accommodation + convergence + miosis
• Corneal reflex = V1 in → VII out
• VOR and MLF: Coordinate eye movements; MLF lesions cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
